summary.title: On Call Rotations: How Best to Wake Devs Up in the Middle of the Night
summary.one_liner: Charity Majors' advice on running software on-call rotations that engineers see as an honor, not a burden: give each rotation an owner, treat code as a liability, and page people only when the world is on fire.
keywords: who should be paged at night
takeaways: Put engineers on call to build ownership and align infrastructure with DevOps; on-call keeps teams close to customer needs and maintenance.
Give every rotation an owner, usually a manager, who follows up on pages so the root cause gets fixed.
Treat code as a liability: prefer fixing problems within the existing codebase over adding new code.
Use on-call time to fix support tickets, flaky tests, staging and security reports; page people only when the world is on fire.
Managers should step out of the rotation and cover for engineers after a rough night, and avoid paging new parents.
summary.summary: This article reports on a talk by Charity Majors, founder of Honeycomb, given at Monki Gras in London, about sustainable on-call practices in software teams. It frames on-call as essential to maintainability and shared ownership of a codebase, and offers five tips: assign a rotation owner, treat code as a liability, treat services as owned rather than operated, use on-call time to fix small problems, and show real appreciation. The piece is opinion and conference recap rather than a how-to with tools or data, so its guidance is general and managerial.
